genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a technician looks after an optical instrument set up high on a plateau
she does her work through the night
the site was picked well away from town lighting
grime on the mirror blunted the sharpness of the images
frequent washing would have damaged the reflecting surface
with a mechanic she designed a movable screen triggered by the wind
the arrangement kept the quality of the observations intact
a second one is planned for the instrument next door
text: You could pass this technician in a corridor and never guess that she works right through the night. She looks after a telescope perched on a windy plateau, well away from the glow of any town. Dust was what bothered her, she says. Within a week the mirror would be furred over and the images lost their edge. Washing it often would only have worn the reflecting surface away, so she went looking elsewhere. Together with a mechanic she rigged up a soft screen that swings shut the moment the wind gets up. The mirror has kept its gleam ever since, and the pictures come out crisp. She laughs as she tells it, as though anyone would have hit on the same trick. Her colleagues know better: the idea rescued whole nights of watching. She is putting together a second screen now, for the instrument next door.

units: two halls for projecting the night sky have opened in the same region
the first one banks on visual intensity
that intensity wears the viewer out instead of teaching anything
the second hall takes a plainer approach
its spoken commentary describes how orbits work
the passage given over to comets exposes the gap between the two
the entry prices are much the same
the writer plainly recommends the second hall
the second hall also runs a session with no spoken commentary
text: Two halls given over to projecting the night sky have opened in one and the same region, and the comparison falls firmly to the second of them. The first trades on sheer force: its dome buries you under a torrent of stars so fierce that it dazzles far more than it teaches. You come out giddy, carrying nothing away. The second holds back. Its darker vault lets the eye breathe, and the telling rests on a voice that explains the workings of orbits rather than dressing them up. The gap opens wide during the passage on comets: where one piles on effects, the other calmly shows a frozen core warming as it nears its star. Entry costs much the same at either door. The second also runs a silent session, given over to nothing but quiet. The choice between them, though, is anything but quiet.

units: the writer is on a terrace she used to visit with the friend she is addressing
she keeps three sights from the evening
the shade of the dusk fades away behind a ridge
a satellite crosses the sky without a sound
the pale trail of our galaxy strikes her as impossible to describe
she still has a star chart given to her long ago
that chart helps her find again the constellations she was taught
she asks her friend to come back
she spoke aloud to her absent friend
text: I am writing from the terrace we used to climb up to, and the sky here is as wide as you remember it. Three sights held me this evening. First the colour of the dusk, turning violet before it faded out behind the ridge. Then a satellite going over, a patient dot that slid across the vault without a sound and without any glare. Last of all the silvery dust of our galaxy, which I can never describe without betraying its softness. I brought your old star chart with me, the one whose folds have worn transparent. It still helps me pick out the shapes you taught me. A warm wind carried the smell of dry grass, and I caught myself talking to you out loud. Nothing up there has changed, and that steadies me more than I expected. Come back whenever you like: the terrace is waiting, and so am I.

units: lift-off begins once the thrust exceeds the weight of the whole stack
the opening phase serves to clear the dense layers of the atmosphere
the lower stage separates once its propellant is spent
that stage falls back into a stretch of sea set aside beforehand
the launcher then tilts its path
that tilt supplies the sideways speed an orbit requires
the fairing opens when air friction has become negligible
the payload separates and makes contact with a station on the ground
the phases are driven by physical thresholds and not by a timetable
text: People often ask what happens in the half hour that follows a launch, and the answer comes as a strict run of stages. The launcher lifts off the moment thrust exceeds the weight of the whole stack; those first seconds are spent clearing the dense layers of the atmosphere in a blazing plume. Then the lower stage parts company, its propellant spent. Where does it go? It drops back into an open stretch of sea, set aside beforehand. Must the vehicle turn at that point? It must: it tilts its path to build sideways speed, since an orbit is held by speed and not by height. The fairing opens once air friction has become negligible. The payload comes away at last, and its aerial reaches for the ground station that will follow it. Every stage fires on a measured threshold, never on a time fixed in advance.

units: the operations manager announces that a manoeuvre is put back
a flare on the nearby star has loaded the upper atmosphere with particles
that load disturbs the radio links
an engineer asks whether the docking can go ahead all the same
the manager refuses and gives grounds for his decision
without a steady link the automatic pilot no longer receives its corrections
a crew member points out that the water reserves are ample
the manoeuvre will resume once the flow of particles has eased
text: The operations manager let the crew know that the manoeuvre would have to be put back. He explained that a flare on the nearest star had loaded the upper atmosphere with particles, and that the radio links were suffering for it. The flight engineer asked whether the craft might dock all the same before the rotation ended. The manager turned the request down and set out his grounds for it: without a steady link the automatic pilot would stop receiving its corrections, and the approach would turn hazardous. One crew member pointed out that the water reserves were ample, with a good margin to spare. The manager concluded that waiting would therefore cost nothing beyond a little patience, and that the manoeuvre would begin again as soon as the flow of particles had eased off.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: angle measurements differed from one observer to the next
wooden instruments warped in damp air
the unaided eye limited how fine a reading could be
metal replaced wood to gain in steadiness
fitting a small telescope to the moving arm cut the error tenfold
it became clear that the date and the warmth of the air had to be written down
those notes served to correct the effects of expansion afterwards
astronomy became in this way a rigorous discipline of measurement
observation notebooks survive and bear witness to that habit
text: The earliest astronomers ran up against a stubborn difficulty: their angle measurements differed from one observer to the next, and nobody could settle the matter. Wooden instruments warped in damp air, and the unaided eye could not fix a position beyond a certain fineness. The remedy arrived in stages. Wood gave way first to metal, which held its shape far better. A small telescope was then fitted to the moving arm, and the error fell to a tenth of what it had been. At last it grew plain that every sighting had to be written down with its date and the warmth of the air, so that the effects of expansion could be corrected afterwards. That habit of the written note changed the trade: astronomy stopped being an art of looking and became a science of measuring. The surviving notebooks record it page after page, in a cramped hand.

units: an asteroid is a dry dense lump
it has circled close to its star since the system formed
its shape alters little despite the rounds of heating and cooling
a comet comes from the far cold reaches
it mixes ice with rocky debris
on nearing the star its ice turns straight into gas
that change gives rise to a long tail
the two objects bear witness to the same ancient origin
the tail points away from the star whatever the direction of travel
text: Want to get the difference between an asteroid and a comet? Picture two stones. The first is dry, dense and dusty, and it has circled close to its star since the system was born. It barely alters: heated, cooled, it holds its shape. The second comes from much further out, from the black cold of the outer reaches. It carries ice mixed in with grit. While it drifts out there it looks a lot like the first. But the moment it draws near, its ice turns straight into gas and it trails an enormous tail behind it, stretching across huge distances. That is the gap: one is a lump of rock, the other a block of ice that shows itself by melting. One detail is worth adding: the tail points away from the star whichever way the thing is heading. Both tell the same old story, but only the second puts on a show.

units: a power cut left a district without lighting
neighbours who never spoke to one another sat down together to watch the sky
a retired teacher set his telescope up on a roof
he showed the rings of a planet to some children
a checkout assistant photographed the night sky with her phone
her picture showed a blurred but recognisable streak
the current came back at sunrise
a good many witnesses were sorry it had returned
the network operator puts the cut down to a defective transformer
text: The power cut that dropped a whole district into darkness turned out to have an unexpected effect. Three scenes tell it. In a courtyard, neighbours who had never once spoken to each other ended up sitting side by side, heads tipped back, counting the stars that had sprung up all at once. On a nearby roof, a retired teacher fetched his telescope and improvised a session; he showed the rings of a pale planet to children who had never seen anything of the kind. Outside a darkened cinema, a checkout assistant photographed the vault with her phone and got, to her own surprise, a blurred but recognisable streak. The current came back at sunrise. The network operator blamed the cut on a defective transformer. Plenty of witnesses admitted they were almost sorry to see the lights return.

units: a night with no moonlight has to be chosen
the eyes need a long spell of adjusting to the dark
the watcher lies down on a blanket before sweeping the sky with his gaze
he follows a shape he has spotted until he ties it to a figure he knows
the star chart is opened only after that step
a red filter protects night vision
a shooting star may appear towards the east late in the watch
the gear is put away before the damp gets at it
observations are worth writing down before going to sleep
text: Pick a night without a moon, and a height from which the eye can run free. Let your sight settle into the dark: it needs a long stretch of patience before the faint stars come through. Spread a blanket, lie down, and let your gaze wander the vault without trying yet to name a thing. When a shape stands out, follow it until it joins some figure you already know. Only then open your chart, shielded by a red filter that spares your night vision. Compare, doubt, begin again. Towards the end of the watch, turn to the east: a shooting star crosses there now and then and burns out in a brief streak. Write down what you saw before you sleep, or else the next watch will blur the memory of it. Put your gear away before the damp can get at it, and go back down again without hurrying.

units: the number of satellites in low orbit is climbing steeply
each satellite throws the light of the central star back towards the ground
its passage across a sensor leaves a bright mark on the exposure
that mark saturates the sensitive elements concerned
faint bodies lying behind it become impossible to detect
teams have to discard the frame or rebuild it by computation
one observatory found that one exposure in ten was affected early in the night
makers are darkening the exposed surfaces
the first trials halve the light thrown back
text: The growing number of satellites in low orbit now weighs heavily on astronomical records, and the mechanism behind it is well understood. Each craft throws the light of the central star back towards the ground; when it crosses the field of a sensor during a long exposure, it writes a bright trail across it. That trail saturates the sensitive elements it touches, which blots out the faint bodies lying behind it. Teams must then throw the frame away, or rebuild the lost patch by computation, and both answers are costly. One observatory has measured that one exposure in ten is affected early in the night. Makers are answering by darkening the exposed surfaces, and the first trials halve the light thrown back. For wide-field instruments the trouble remains entirely unsolved.
